title: Foul mudammas
subtitle: Egyptian spiced fava beans
excerpt: Slow-cooked fava beans mashed with lemon, garlic, cumin, and olive oil. The national breakfast dish of Egypt and the Middle East, eaten with flatbread, sliced tomato, and hard-boiled egg.
sourceNotes: Foul mudammas is one of the oldest documented cooked dishes in the world, mentioned in medieval Arabic culinary manuscripts. Cross-referenced with Claudia Roden, The New Book of Middle Eastern Food (2000) for proportions and regional variations.

recipe.batchNotes: Doubles well. Keeps in the fridge for 3 days; the flavour improves by the second day.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the day before and reheat gently with a splash of water.

content.text: Foul mudammas is cooked fava beans, roughly mashed with lemon juice, garlic, cumin, and olive oil. It is the street-food breakfast of Egypt, eaten with flatbread, fresh tomato, and boiled egg. The combination of starchy beans, sharp lemon, earthy cumin, and good olive oil is simple and filling.

items.prepNote: two 400 g tins of fava beans, drained and rinsed; or 250 g dried fava beans soaked overnight and cooked until tender
crushed to a paste with a little salt

content.text: Put the drained beans in a saucepan with enough water to barely cover. Warm over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until heated through. The water should reduce slightly.

Remove from heat. Roughly mash about half the beans with a fork or masher, leaving some whole for texture. Add the garlic paste, lemon juice, cumin, and most of the olive oil. Stir well. The mixture should be thick and slightly creamy, not a smooth purée.
Taste and adjust: more lemon for brightness, more cumin for earthiness, salt to taste. The seasoning should be assertive.

Spoon the beans into shallow bowls. Drizzle with the remaining olive oil, scatter over the parsley and a pinch of chilli flakes if using. A dust of ground cumin goes on top. Serve immediately with warm pitta, sliced tomato, and hard-boiled eggs.

items.symptom: The beans taste flat and starchy
items.fix: Add more lemon juice a squeeze at a time. The acidity lifts the dish entirely.

items.cause: The water cooked off too fast
items.fix: Add a splash of the bean cooking water or plain water and stir.

items.symptom: The garlic is too raw and sharp
items.cause: The garlic was not crushed to a fine paste
items.fix: Crush garlic to a paste with a pinch of salt using the flat of a knife. The salt helps break it down.

items.symptom: The dish is too thick and heavy
items.fix: Leave more whole beans for texture. Thin with a little warm water.

content.text: Foul mudammas is eaten from Morocco to the Gulf, but Egypt is its heartland. In Cairo it is sold from carts and restaurants as early as 5am, cooked in large clay pots that have been on the heat since the previous evening. The word mudammas means 'buried', a reference to the old tradition of burying the sealed pot in the embers of dying fires to cook slowly overnight. It is one of the few dishes that crosses all social boundaries in Egypt: eaten by everyone, everywhere.
